source.title: Let's Agree to Agree: Neural Networks Share Classification Order on Real Datasets
source.authors: Guy Hacohen; Leshem Choshen; Daphna Weinshall

record.tranche_reason: The paper measures agreement in per-example classification and the order in which examples are learned. These are related to model similarity, but do not measure representational distances, features, or mappings named by the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper's own classification-agreement and learning-order results are recorded as findings about a related construct under fits_no_version. They do not test any listed version of representational convergence. The paper also cites prior representational-similarity findings; those cited results are not rows.
record.test_reason: The paper measures per-example classification agreement (TP-agreement, Agreement score) and learning order (accessibility score) across independently trained networks. These are output or functional similarity measures. It reports no representational similarity, feature, subspace, mapping or stitching measure, and no scaling or cross-modal analysis. It only cites representational-similarity work (Li et al., Raghu et al., Morcos et al.), so it tests none of V1–V7. Its findings go under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is essentially correct. Two points should be added. Stronger architectures first learn the examples that weaker ones learn (ResNet-50 vs AlexNet; non-linear vs linear st-VGG), then learn additional examples. The authors hypothesise that this reflects how networks discover structure common to natural datasets.
record.recipe_differences: The paper measures classification correctness and example-learning order, not the representational-similarity methods in the cited original sources.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported classification-order pattern changes with dataset conditions: it is absent or weaker on synthetic Gabor data, shuffled-label data, and the Gaussian task; out-of-sample prediction agreement varies with image naturalness and similarity to training data.

fits_no_version.finding: On real benchmarks, independently initialized networks of the same architecture classify the same examples correctly and learn them in the same order. Agreement across architectures is high (accessibility r = 0.78–0.99). The pattern holds for collections trained on disjoint partitions drawn from the same distribution.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Independently trained neural networks share per-example classification order on natural datasets, within and across architectures.

fits_no_version.finding: The shared order disappears on synthetic Gabor and Gaussian data and on shuffled labels. It reappears only partially on the Gabor test set. AdaBoost's learning order correlates weakly with the networks' order (r = 0.35 on pixels, 0.05 on Inception-V3 features).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Shared learning order depends on how neural networks interact with natural data structure. It is not a universal property of classifiers or of SGD.

fits_no_version.finding: Prediction agreement on out-of-sample images is always above the random-label level. It rises as images become more natural and closer to the training distribution.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Cross-model prediction agreement depends on the input distribution.

fits_no_version.finding: Linear st-VGG also shows bi-modal TP-agreement, more strongly than non-linear st-VGG. Non-linear networks first learn the examples linear networks learn, then go on to new ones.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Shared classification order does not require non-linearity.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 37th International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 119, 2020
record.problems: The measured construct is classification agreement and learning order rather than representational similarity. The paper does not test model-size or capability scaling. Many results are qualitative distributions; several reported correlations have p-values but no confidence intervals stated in the text.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted repeated qualitative TP-agreement plots for additional benchmark dataset and architecture combinations in Supplementary Figs. 13–21 and 28, and repeated AdaBoost dataset comparisons in Supplementary §F; these are described by the paper as showing the same qualitative pattern.

untested.parts: Representational alignment across independently trained models as size or capability grows. Only classification-order agreement is measured.
Shared features or subspaces across seeds. Agreement on which examples are classified correctly is not a feature or subspace measure.
Linear maps, stitching, relative representations or unpaired mapping between models.
Recurrence of interpretable neurons, SAE features or circuits across models.
Dependence of representational similarity on the metric, its settings or the inputs. Input dependence is shown only for prediction agreement (R19–R22).
Whether representational alignment is incomplete or plateaus, and whether shared data or objectives explain it.

record.verdict_notes: Relation stays 'discusses' / T6. The paper discusses the representational-similarity literature but measures only output-level agreement, a related but different construct. It has no verdict labels. Some results are not rowed: the Fig. 8a/25 overlap curves, AlexNet vs DenseNet r = 0.87 (Fig. 26), and the Agreement-score results in Fig. 5. These fall under fits_no_version, not any version, so they are not listed as missing.

versions.untested_parts: Model size and capability scaling, and representational alignment between independently trained models.
Vision-language alignment on paired images and captions, and its relationship to model performance.
Shared features or subspaces across seeds; classification agreement is not a feature or subspace measure.
Mapping, stitching, relative representations, or unpaired interchangeability.
Recurrence of interpretable features or circuits across models.
Sensitivity of representational convergence to similarity metrics, settings, and input distributions.
Whether representational alignment plateaus or is explained by shared data or objectives rather than a common model of reality.

rows.subject: ResNet-50
rows.operation_detail: Measured TP-agreement across independently initialized models during training.
rows.measure: Distribution of per-example TP-agreement over epochs
rows.baseline: Independent random classification vectors with matching accuracy; described as approximately Gaussian.
rows.value: The real-model distribution becomes bi-modal after a few epochs and remains so through learning; models classify the same examples correctly and consistently misclassify the same examples.
rows.note: The stated outcome concerns classification behavior, not representational distances.

rows.measure: Distribution of per-example TP-agreement over epochs
rows.baseline: not stated
rows.value: The train and test datasets are described as being learned in the same order; the distribution is shown for both.
rows.note: Classification order is not a measure of representation alignment.

rows.note: This is the paper's stated aggregate pattern across benchmarks; it does not report a single pooled numerical estimate.

rows.subject: Linear st-VGG
rows.measure: Maximum Pearson bi-modality score of TP-agreement distribution
rows.baseline: Non-linear st-VGG maximum Pearson bi-modality score: 0.06
rows.value: Maximum Pearson bi-modality score: 0.22; distribution described as bi-modal.
rows.note: The comparison concerns classification agreement; the paper says linear networks converge faster and have weaker performance.
rows.check: The values are swapped. The text gives linear st-VGG a maximum Pearson bi-modality of 0.06 and non-linear st-VGG 0.22. Lower means more bi-modal, so the linear case is more bi-modal. Value should be 0.06 and baseline should be non-linear 0.22.

rows.check: The values are swapped. Non-linear st-VGG's maximum Pearson bi-modality is 0.22, not 0.06; the baseline should be linear st-VGG at 0.06.

rows.subject: st-VGG
rows.baseline: Natural benchmark datasets, where the paper reports bi-modal distributions.

rows.note: This is a counterexample to the paper's classification-order pattern, not a test of representational convergence.
